title: Chapter 12. Of Religion
paragraphs: Since there are no signs or fruits of religion except in man, there is no reason to doubt that the seed of religion is also found only in man. It consists in some peculiar quality, or at least in some eminent degree of one, that is not to be found in other living creatures.

First, it is peculiar to human nature to be inquisitive into the causes of the events people see — some more, some less, but every person enough to be curious about the causes of their own good and bad fortune.
Second, when men see anything that has a beginning, they think it must also have had a cause that determined it to start exactly when it did, rather than sooner or later.

Third, whereas beasts have no other happiness than the enjoyment of their daily food, rest, and lusts — having little or no foresight of the time to come, for lack of observation and memory of the order, sequence, and dependence of the things they see — man observes how one event has been produced by another, and remembers in such things their antecedence and consequence. And when he cannot be sure of the true causes of things (for the causes of good and bad fortune are for the most part invisible), he supposes causes of them, either such as his own fancy suggests, or he trusts to the authority of other men whom he thinks to be his friends and wiser than himself.

[The Natural Cause Of Religion: The Anxiety Of The Time To Come.] The first two of these make for anxiety. For being assured that there are causes of all things that have happened up to now, or shall happen hereafter, it is impossible for a man who continually tries to secure himself against the evil he fears and to procure the good he desires not to be in perpetual concern about the time to come. So every man, especially those who are too provident, is in a state much like that of Prometheus. For as Prometheus (which, interpreted, means The Prudent Man) was bound to the hill Caucasus, a place of wide prospect, where an eagle feeding on his liver devoured by day as much as was repaired by night, so the man who looks too far ahead in care for the future has his heart gnawed all day long by fear of death, poverty, or other calamity; and he has no rest, no pause in his anxiety, except in sleep.

This perpetual fear, always accompanying mankind in the ignorance of causes — as though it walked in the dark — must have some object. And therefore when there is nothing to be seen, there is nothing to credit for one's good or bad fortune except some invisible power or agent. It was perhaps in this sense that some of the old poets said that the gods were first created by human fear; which, said of the gods (that is, of the many gods of the Gentiles), is quite true. But the acknowledgment of one God, eternal, infinite, and omnipotent, may more easily be derived from people's desire to know the causes of natural bodies and their several powers and operations, than from the fear of what might happen to them in time to come. For anyone who, from some effect he sees come to pass, reasons to its next and immediate cause, and from that to the cause of that cause, plunging himself deeply into the pursuit of causes, must at last arrive at this: there must be (as even the heathen philosophers confessed) one First Mover — that is, a first, eternal cause of all things — which is what men mean by the name of God. And all this without any thought of their fortune, the worry about which both inclines them to fear and hinders them from searching for the causes of other things, and thereby gives them occasion to invent as many gods as there are men who invent them.

As for the matter or substance of the invisible agents thus imagined, men could not, by natural reflection, hit upon any conception of them other than that they were the same as the soul of man; and that the soul of man was of the same substance as that which appears in a dream to one who is asleep, or in a looking-glass to one who is awake. Not knowing that such apparitions are nothing else but creatures of the imagination, men take them to be real and external substances, and therefore call them ghosts — as the Latins called them Imagines and Umbrae — and supposed them to be spirits, that is, thin airy bodies; and supposed those invisible agents which they feared to be like them, except that they appear and vanish as they please. But the opinion that such spirits were incorporeal or immaterial could never enter the mind of any man by nature. For although men may string together words of contradictory meaning — like Spirit and Incorporeal — they can never form any imagination corresponding to them. Therefore, men who through their own meditation arrive at the acknowledgment of one infinite, omnipotent, and eternal God prefer to confess that he is incomprehensible and above their understanding, rather than to define his nature by Spirit Incorporeal and then confess their definition unintelligible. Or if they do give him such a title, it is not dogmatically, with the intention of making the divine nature understood, but piously, to honor him with attributes whose meanings are as remote as possible from the grossness of visible bodies.

Then, as for the way they think these invisible agents brought about their effects — that is, what immediate causes they used to bring things to pass — men who do not know what we call causing (which is almost all men) have no other rule to guess by but observing and remembering what they have seen precede the like effect at some other time or times before, without seeing any dependence or connection at all between the antecedent and the subsequent event. And therefore from like things past they expect like things to come, and hope for good or bad luck, superstitiously, from things that have no part at all in causing it. So the Athenians, for their war at Lepanto, demanded another Phormio; the Pompeian faction, for their war in Africa, another Scipio; and others have done likewise on many other occasions since. In the same way they attribute their fortune to a bystander, to a lucky or unlucky place, to words spoken — especially if the name of God is among them — as in charming and conjuring (the liturgy of witches); to the point of believing that they have power to turn a stone into bread, bread into a man, or anything into anything.

Third, as for the worship which men naturally show toward invisible powers, it can be no other than such expressions of reverence as they would use toward men: gifts, petitions, thanks, bowing of the body, considered addresses, sober behavior, premeditated words, and swearing (that is, assuring one another of their promises) by invoking them. Beyond that reason suggests nothing, but leaves them either to rest there, or, for further ceremonies, to rely on those they believe to be wiser than themselves.

Lastly, as to how these invisible powers reveal to men things that will come to pass — especially concerning their good or bad fortune in general, or success or failure in any particular undertaking — men are naturally at a loss. Except that, being accustomed to guess at the time to come by the time past, they are very apt not only to take chance occurrences, after one or two encounters, as predictions of the like ever after, but also to accept like predictions from other men of whom they have once formed a good opinion.

And in these four things — belief in ghosts, ignorance of secondary causes, devotion toward what men fear, and taking chance events as omens — consists the natural seed of religion. Because of the different fancies, judgments, and passions of different people, it has grown up into ceremonies so different that those used by one man are for the most part ridiculous to another.

For these seeds have been cultivated by two sorts of men. One sort have nourished and ordered them according to their own invention. The other have done it by God's commandment and direction. But both sorts have done it with the same purpose: to make the men who relied on them more disposed to obedience, laws, peace, charity, and civil society. So the religion of the first sort is a part of human politics, and teaches part of the duty earthly kings require of their subjects. The religion of the second sort is divine politics, and contains precepts for those who have yielded themselves as subjects in the kingdom of God. Of the first sort were all the founders of commonwealths and the law-givers of the Gentiles. Of the second sort were Abraham, Moses, and our Blessed Saviour, by whom have been delivered to us the laws of the kingdom of God.

As for that part of religion which consists in opinions about the nature of invisible powers, there is almost nothing that has a name which has not, among the Gentiles, somewhere or other, been esteemed a god or a devil, or imagined by their poets to be animate, inhabited, or possessed by some spirit or other.
The unformed matter of the world was a god, under the name of Chaos.
The heaven, the ocean, the planets, the fire, the earth, the winds were so many gods.

Men, women, a bird, a crocodile, a calf, a dog, a snake, an onion, a leek were all deified. Besides, they filled almost every place with spirits called daemons: the plains with Pan and the Panises, or Satyrs; the woods with Fauns and Nymphs; the sea with Tritons and other nymphs; every river and fountain with a ghost of its own name, and with nymphs; every house with its Lares, or household spirits; every man with his Genius; hell with ghosts and spiritual officers such as Charon, Cerberus, and the Furies; and at night every place with Larvae, Lemures, ghosts of the dead, and a whole kingdom of fairies and bugbears. They also ascribed divinity, and built temples, to mere accidents and qualities — such as Time, Night, Day, Peace, Concord, Love, Strife, Virtue, Honor, Health, Rust, Fever, and the like — which, when they prayed for them or against them, they prayed to as if there were ghosts of those names hovering over their heads, letting fall or withholding the good or evil for or against which they prayed. They also invoked their own wit, by the name of the Muses; their own ignorance, by the name of Fortune; their own lust, by the name of Cupid; their own rage, by the name of the Furies; their own private parts, by the name of Priapus; and they attributed their pollutions to Incubi and Succubae — so that there was nothing a poet could introduce as a character in his poem that they did not make into either a god or a devil.

The same authors of the religion of the Gentiles, observing the second ground of religion — namely men's ignorance of causes, and their consequent readiness to attribute their fortune to causes on which there was no apparent dependence — took the opportunity to foist on this ignorance, in place of secondary causes, a kind of second-rank, ministering gods: ascribing fertility to Venus, the arts to Apollo, subtlety and craft to Mercury, tempests and storms to Aeolus, and other effects to other gods — so that among the heathen there was almost as great a variety of gods as of occupations.

And to the worship which men naturally thought fit to use toward their gods — namely oblations, prayers, thanks, and the rest already named — the same legislators of the Gentiles added images of them, both in painting and in sculpture, so that the more ignorant sort (that is, the greater part of the people), thinking that the gods the images represented were really included, as it were housed within them, might stand all the more in fear of them. They endowed them with lands, houses, officers, and revenues, set apart from all other human uses — that is, consecrated and made holy to these idols — such as caverns, groves, woods, mountains, and whole islands. And they attributed to them not only shapes (of men, of beasts, of monsters), but also the faculties and passions of men and beasts: sense, speech, sex, lust, generation (and this not only by mixing with one another to propagate the kind of gods, but also by mixing with men and women to beget mongrel gods, mere lodgers in heaven, such as Bacchus, Hercules, and others); besides anger, revenge, and other passions of living creatures, and the actions proceeding from them — fraud, theft, adultery, sodomy, and any vice that may be taken either as an effect of power or as a cause of pleasure; and all such vices as, among men, are considered to be against law rather than against honor.

Lastly, to the prognostics of the time to come (which are naturally only conjectures based on past experience, and supernaturally divine revelation), the same authors of the religion of the Gentiles added, partly on pretended experience and partly on pretended revelation, innumerable other superstitious forms of divination. They made men believe they might find their fortunes sometimes in the ambiguous or senseless answers of the priests at Delphi, Delos, Ammon, and other famous oracles — answers made ambiguous by design, so that the event could be claimed either way, or made absurd by the intoxicating vapor of the place, which is very common in sulphurous caverns. Sometimes in the leaves of the Sibyls (whose prophecies — like those perhaps of Nostradamus, for the surviving fragments seem to be of later invention — had some books of repute in the time of the Roman Republic). Sometimes in the meaningless speeches of madmen, supposed to be possessed by a divine spirit (which possession they called Enthusiasm); and these kinds of foretelling were called Theomancy, or prophecy. Sometimes in the aspect of the stars at one's birth, which was called Horoscopy and counted a branch of judicial astrology. Sometimes in their own hopes and fears, called Thumomancy, or presage. Sometimes in the predictions of witches, who claimed to confer with the dead — which is called Necromancy, Conjuring, and Witchcraft, and is nothing but trickery and collusive fraud. Sometimes in the chance flight or feeding of birds, called Augury. Sometimes in the entrails of a sacrificed beast, which was Aruspicina. Sometimes in dreams. Sometimes in the croaking of ravens, or the chattering of birds. Sometimes in the features of the face, which was called Metoposcopy; or by Palmistry, in the lines of the hand; in chance words, called Omina. Sometimes in monsters or unusual accidents — such as eclipses, comets, rare meteors, earthquakes, floods, strange births, and the like — which they called Portenta and Ostenta because they were thought to portend or foreshow some great calamity to come. Sometimes in mere lottery, like heads or tails (Cross and Pile), counting holes in a sieve, dipping into verses of Homer and Virgil, and innumerable other empty conceits. So easily are men drawn to believe anything from such men as have gained credit with them, and who can with gentleness and dexterity take hold of their fear and ignorance.

[The Designs Of The Authors Of The Religion Of The Heathen.] And therefore the first founders and legislators of commonwealths among the Gentiles, whose aims were only to keep the people in obedience and peace, have everywhere taken care: First, to imprint in their minds a belief that the precepts they gave concerning religion should not be thought to come from their own invention but from the dictates of some god or other spirit — or else that they themselves were of a higher nature than mere mortals — so that their laws might more easily be received. Thus Numa Pompilius pretended to receive the ceremonies he established among the Romans from the nymph Egeria; the first king and founder of the kingdom of Peru pretended that he and his wife were children of the Sun; and Mahomet, to set up his new religion, pretended to have conferences with the Holy Ghost, in the form of a dove. Second, they took care to have it believed that the same things were displeasing to the gods which were forbidden by the laws. Third, to prescribe ceremonies, supplications, sacrifices, and festivals, by which they were to believe the anger of the gods might be appeased; and that bad success in war, great epidemics, earthquakes, and every man's private misery came from the anger of the gods, and their anger from the neglect of their worship, or from forgetting or mistaking some point of the required ceremonies. And although among the ancient Romans men were not forbidden to deny what the poets wrote of the pains and pleasures after this life — which many of great authority and gravity in that state openly derided in their public speeches — yet that belief was always more cherished than its opposite.

And by these and other such institutions, they obtained, in service of their end (which was the peace of the commonwealth), this: that the common people in their misfortunes, blaming neglect or error in their ceremonies, or their own disobedience to the laws, were less apt to mutiny against their governors. And being entertained with the pomp and pastime of festivals and public games made in honor of the gods, they needed nothing else but bread to keep them from discontent, murmuring, and uprising against the state. And therefore the Romans, having conquered the greatest part of the then-known world, made no scruple of tolerating any religion whatsoever in the City of Rome itself, unless it had something in it inconsistent with their civil government. Nor do we read that any religion was forbidden there except that of the Jews, who (being the peculiar kingdom of God) thought it unlawful to acknowledge subjection to any mortal king or state whatsoever. And thus you see how the religion of the Gentiles was a part of their policy.

[The True Religion, And The Laws Of God's Kingdom The Same.] But where God himself, by supernatural revelation, planted religion, there he also made for himself a peculiar kingdom, and gave laws — not only of behavior toward himself but also toward one another. And thereby in the kingdom of God, policy and the civil laws are a part of religion, and so the distinction between temporal and spiritual dominion has no place there. It is true that God is king of all the earth; yet he may be king of a particular, chosen nation. For there is no more incongruity in this than that one who holds the general command of the whole army should also have his own particular regiment or company. God is king of all the earth by his power, but of his chosen people he is king by covenant. But I have assigned another place in the following discourse to speak more fully of the kingdom of God, both by nature and by covenant.

From the way religion is propagated, it is not hard to understand the causes by which it dissolves back into its first seeds or principles — which are only an opinion of a deity and of powers invisible and supernatural. These can never be so abolished out of human nature but that new religions may once again spring out of them, by the cultivation of such men as are held in repute for that purpose.

For since all formed religion is founded at first upon the faith that a multitude has in some one person, whom they believe not only to be a wise man, laboring to procure their happiness, but also a holy man, to whom God himself vouchsafes to declare his will supernaturally, it follows necessarily that when those who govern religion come to have their wisdom suspected, or their sincerity, or their love; or when they are unable to show any plausible token of divine revelation, the religion they would uphold must also be suspected, and (without the fear of the civil sword) contradicted and rejected.

What takes away the reputation of wisdom in someone who forms a religion, or adds to it once it has been formed, is the demand that men believe contradictions. For both sides of a contradiction cannot possibly be true; and so to enjoin belief in them is a sign of ignorance, which exposes the author in that, and discredits him in everything else he may propose as coming from supernatural revelation. A man may indeed have revelation of many things above natural reason, but of nothing against it.

What takes away the reputation of sincerity is the doing or saying of such things as appear to be signs that what they require other men to believe is not believed by themselves. All such doings or sayings are therefore called Scandalous, because they are stumbling-blocks that make men fall in the way of religion: injustice, cruelty, profaneness, avarice, and luxury. For who can believe that someone who ordinarily does the kinds of things that proceed from any of these roots really believes there is any such invisible power to be feared as he uses to frighten other men over lesser faults?

What takes away the reputation of love is the discovery of private ends — as when the belief they require of others tends, or seems to tend, to acquiring dominion, riches, dignity, or secure pleasure for themselves alone or especially. For what men gain advantage by for themselves, they are thought to do for their own sake, and not out of love for others.

Lastly, the testimony men can give of a divine calling can be nothing other than the working of miracles; or true prophecy (which is also a miracle); or extraordinary felicity. And therefore, in addition to those points of religion that have been received from people who did such miracles, the points added by those who do not approve their calling by any miracle gain no greater belief than what the custom and laws of the places where they were brought up have instilled in them. For as in natural things men of judgment require natural signs and arguments, so in supernatural things they require supernatural signs (which are miracles) before they assent inwardly and from their hearts.

All these causes of the weakening of men's faith are clearly apparent in the following examples. First, we have the example of the children of Israel, who, when Moses (who had proved his calling to them by miracles and by the happy leading of them out of Egypt) was absent only forty days, revolted from the worship of the true God that he had commended to them, and setting up (Exod. 32:1,2) a Golden Calf for their God, relapsed into the idolatry of the Egyptians, from whom they had been so recently delivered. And again, after Moses, Aaron, Joshua, and the generation that had seen the great works of God in Israel were dead (Judges 2:11), another generation arose and served Baal. So that, miracles failing, faith also failed.

Again, when the sons of Samuel (1 Sam. 8:3), having been appointed by their father as judges in Beersheba, took bribes and judged unjustly, the people of Israel refused any longer to have God as their king in any way different from how he was king of other peoples, and therefore cried out to Samuel to choose them a king after the manner of the nations. So that, justice failing, faith also failed — to the point that they deposed their God from reigning over them.

And whereas in the planting of the Christian religion the oracles ceased in every part of the Roman Empire, and the number of Christians increased wonderfully every day and in every place by the preaching of the Apostles and Evangelists, a great part of that success may reasonably be attributed to the contempt into which the priests of the Gentiles of that time had brought themselves, by their uncleanness, avarice, and dealings between princes. Also the religion of the Church of Rome was, partly for the same reason, abolished in England and in many other parts of Christendom — so that the failing of virtue in the pastors makes faith fail in the people. And partly it was abolished because of the bringing of the philosophy and doctrine of Aristotle into religion by the schoolmen, from which there arose so many contradictions and absurdities that they brought the clergy into a reputation both of ignorance and of fraudulent intention, inclining people to revolt from them — either against the will of their own princes, as in France and Holland, or with their will, as in England.

Lastly, among the points the Church of Rome declares necessary for salvation, there are so many manifestly to the advantage of the Pope and of his spiritual subjects residing in the territories of other Christian princes, that were it not for the mutual rivalry of those princes, they might without war or trouble exclude all foreign authority as easily as it has been excluded in England. For who is there that does not see whose benefit it serves to have it believed: that a king has no authority from Christ unless a bishop crowns him? That a king, if he is a priest, cannot marry? That whether a prince is born in lawful marriage or not must be judged by authority from Rome? That subjects may be freed from their allegiance if, by the Court of Rome, the king is judged a heretic? That a king (like Chilperic of France) may be deposed by a pope (like Pope Zachary) for no cause, and his kingdom given to one of his subjects? That the clergy and the regulars, in whatever country, shall be exempt from the jurisdiction of their king in criminal cases? Or who does not see to whose profit accrue the fees of private masses, and the takings of purgatory, with other signs of private interest — enough to mortify the most lively faith, if (as I said) the civil magistrate and custom did not sustain it more than any opinion they have of the sanctity, wisdom, or probity of their teachers? So that I may attribute all the changes of religion in the world to one and the same cause: displeasing priests — and not only among Catholics, but even in that church which has presumed most of reformation.
